Zii Jia will face France's world No 51 shuttler Arnaud Merkle for a place in the semi-finals.
Also through to the last eight is world No 48 women's singles shuttler Wong Ling Ching who beat lower-ranked home player Tanya Hemanth 16-21, 21-13, 21-17 in 59 minutes.
She will face Thailand's world No 26 and fourth-seeded player Supanida Katethong in the last eight match tomorrow.
Separately, young mixed doubles pair Wee Yee Hern-Vannee Gobi, ranked 61st, shocked top seeds and world No 24 pair Dhruv Kapila-Tanisha Crasto of India 22-20, 21-15 in 40 minutes.
The Malaysians will take on Indonesia's Nawaf Khoiriyansyah-Indah Cahya Sari Jamil, who are ranked 144th, in the quarter-final tomorrow.

7ada5ec3997421d7: 1Password is reassuring customers that their vaults remain secure after an attacker breached its systems and stole account information and private source code.

The Canadian security biz disclosed this week that an attacker had compromised an employee's corporate GitHub account, made off with private source code, and deployed malicious code to its backend services to siphon off customer information.

1Password, which began investigating the intrusion on November 19, hasn't said how many customers were affected, but confirmed that the stolen data includes names and email addresses used to sign in to the service, account identifiers, timestamps showing when users created and last accessed their accounts, and various pieces of non-secret account metadata.

The company insists the information that customers actually pay it to protect was beyond the intruder's reach. "At no time were customer vault contents accessed by, or available to, the attacker," 1Password said.

Arguably more troubling is the revelation that the intruder gained access to 1Password's continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) infrastructure, which houses credentials used to keep its products running. The company says it has rotated or revoked potentially exposed credentials and that neither its apps nor its browser extensions were affected.

1Password hasn't explained how access to an employee's GitHub account enabled the attacker to deploy malicious code to its backend services, nor has it detailed the extent of the attacker's access to its software build and distribution infrastructure. The company did not respond to The Register's questions.

The miscreant also got their hands on tokens embedded in emails sent to some customers as part of account invitations, provisioning, and recovery processes. These tokens aren't enough to access an account on their own, according to 1Password, as users must also authenticate via single sign-on or enter a verification code sent to their registered email address.

The company says it specifically notified the small number of users with affected provisioning or recovery processes underway. It found no internal evidence of account takeovers using the exposed provisioning tokens.

Still, the breach has prompted the password management biz to beef up those verification codes, replacing the six-digit numeric variety with ten-character alphanumeric codes to make brute-forcing them considerably more difficult.

1Password has booted the intruder out of its GitHub environment, revoked the stolen token, and rolled back the affected backend services to clean versions of the code. It's since shored up security around its development infrastructure and employees' devices, and brought in outside security specialists to review its handiwork.

The incident recalls the first stage of LastPass's 2022 breach, when an attacker compromised its development environment and stole source code. Information obtained in that intrusion helped enable a second attack that exposed customer vault backups, including encrypted passwords.

The UK Information Commission's Office slapped LastPass with a £1.2 million ($1.6 million) fine last December over the incident, which compromised the personal information of up to 1.6 million UK users. Among the regulator's gripes was that LastPass had fallen short of the higher standard of security expected of a company entrusted with people's passwords.
Customers aren't being asked to change their account passwords or Secret Keys, neither of which 1Password stores, although the company is warning users to be on the lookout for phishing attempts.

A list of email addresses belonging to people known to use a particular password manager is a handy thing for a phisher to have, especially when said password manager has just given them a plausible pretext for getting in touch. ®

38bebe8b01f35c10: TOKYO, Nov 26 — US President Donald Trump’s fresh tariff blitz aims to pressure Asian countries into sealing trade deals with Washington so as to avoid unfavourable duty rates, analysts said on Thursday.
The proposed levies announced on Wednesday affect a range of nations in the region, from long-time US competitor China to allies like South Korea and Japan.
They could result in rates of up to 20 per cent on exports from the targeted countries, but face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January.

The announcement came after Washington concluded a months-long probe into alleged excess production in the targeted economies, which itself followed the US Supreme Court’s decision ruling that Trump’s previous “Liberation Day” duties were illegal.
But “several of these economies already have prior negotiated tariff rates with the US, which would effectively cap the appliable rate”, said MUFG economist Lloyd Chan in a note.
The US has also indicated that the new tolls will not stack on top of other tariffs already imposed on 60 countries over forced labour concerns. Instead, the higher rate will apply.
“In all, that should help contain the incremental tariff shock, assuming prior negotiated commitment remains in place,” Chan said.
However, it does mean that Washington has established higher tariff ceilings that can be activated “should trade negotiations or existing commitments break down”, he added.
Stephen Brown of Capital Economics also noted that “the US has left open its ability to hike these tariffs if trade agreements fall apart”, particularly with China.
Room for leverage
In Beijing’s case, the new levies stand at 20 per cent, meaning the total rate could jump to 40 per cent if its current trade truce with Washington, set to expire in January, is not extended.
Such a scenario “could take the two largest economies back to the trade wars of 2025”, Josh Lipsky, of the Atlantic Council, wrote in a note.
However, that is not something Trump wants, he added.
Instead, the US president is banking on an extension of the truce, though this is “far from a sure thing”, Lipsky added.
Trump and China’s Xi Jinping are set to meet next in December at the G20 summit in Miami.
“Tariff wars and trade wars are not in anyone’s interest,” Beijing’s foreign ministry warned on Wednesday.
Other Asian economies, also in Trump’s crosshairs due to significant trade imbalances, are likewise under pressure.
Vietnam faces a maximum additional tariff of 35 per cent on goods, which could be cut to 20 per cent if a trade deal is reached.
Hanoi reiterated on Wednesday that it has made commitments under a framework agreement in October 2025, and that it is working for a final deal “as soon as possible”.
India uncertain, Taiwan bullish
India said on Wednesday that trade concerns should be addressed in ongoing talks with Washington for a bilateral trade deal.
The US has proposed a 17 per cent rate on Indian goods, rising to a possible 25 per cent if no deal is reached.
The countries reached an interim agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.
But the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s levies days later, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.

“By deploying a dual-rate structure — threatening steep baseline tariffs against countries that refuse a pact while offering lower rates to those that sign — Washington reclaims the bargaining power to impose duties at will and extract unilateral concessions,” Ajay Srivastava, founder of the Global Trade Research Initiative, told Bloomberg News.
In contrast with Indian uncertainty, Taiwan, which reached a deal with Washington in early 2026, struck a reassuring tone.

“We are confident that when tariffs are finalised early next year, we will return to a 15 per cent non-stacked tariff under the agreement between Taiwan and the US,” Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun told a news briefing. — AFP

18cfa8107ce61490: SC25 in St. Louis looked like a plumbing convention cross booked the supercomputing hall. Pipes, pumps, manifolds, quick-disconnects, and a lot of people who clearly spend more time thinking about pressure drop than floating-point. I kept expecting to see a booth selling industrial fire hoses. Chicago is a much bigger building – McCormick has roughly four times the exhibit space St. Louis had – so the pre-show question was whether SC26 will still look like that or whether the hall is large enough to dilute the effect.
If anything, cooling was even more dominant in Chicago. The heat problem didn't get smaller just because the building got bigger.

We also saw a lot of new companies displaying their cooling wares at SC26. I follow this stuff closely and see two broad trends. First: consolidation with big industrial suppliers buying up the liquid cooling pioneers. Second: anyone with an angle is heading into the market. Both trends were visible on the floor in Chicago, and everyone had something to say about higher inlet temperatures, whether they have a real story or not.
Game changing news

The real news, though, is a number Nvidia dropped earlier this year: 45°C (113°F) liquid inlet temperature for their parts. That's not a small tweak. Most liquid-cooled systems have been living in the 30-35°C (86-95°F) world because that's what the chips would tolerate. Jump to 45°C (113°F) and a whole bunch of datacenters that currently need chillers suddenly don't.

If AMD, Intel, and the Arm folks can match it – and we’d be shocked if they aren't already working on exactly that – then free cooling stops being a cool climate thing and becomes the default for a lot of places.

Rooftop dry coolers can reject nearly any incoming fluid temperature and bring it below 45°C (113°F). There are few places in the world where ambient temperatures approach 113°F, and for the hours when outside temps spike, adiabatic assist is available. This is where water is trickled through a mesh surrounding the dry coolers, which drops the effective temperature another 10–20 percent.

So, in our new cooling world, there are two closed loops: one taking heat from the server gear and then passing it to a second, different loop that takes the hot water to the roof, cools it, then brings it back again.

What's missing here? It's the chillers. You won't need them anymore. These are essentially huge rooftop refrigerators that cool water even more after the dry cooling. They're expensive, need a lot of maintenance, gulp electricity and are thankfully unnecessary now for new datacenter builds.

The power and water savings are not trivial. Legacy designs that rely on chillers and open evaporative towers commonly put 20 percent to 40 percent of total facility energy into cooling. A large share of that is the chiller plant itself – compressors, pumps, and cooling-tower fans. Move to dry coolers running at 45°C (113°F) inlet and that slice collapses.

Published estimates and vendor modeling for high-temperature liquid loops put the reduction in cooling energy in the 50 percent to 70 percent range versus a conventional chiller-plus-tower plant, which translates into a 10 percent to 20 percent drop in total datacenter power – depending on the starting PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness) and climate.

Water use falls even harder. Traditional evaporative towers can consume millions of gallons a year at a mid-size site. Dry coolers use essentially no outside water in normal operation; adiabatic assist only wets the mesh during the hottest hours, cutting annual water consumption by 80 percent to 95 percent in most climates. Those are the numbers that make the 45°C (113°F) inlet such a big deal.

The same shift also changes the economics of the mechanical plant itself. A chiller plant is not just an operating cost; it is capital equipment that has to be sized, installed, maintained, and eventually replaced. Dry coolers are simpler, cheaper to install, and have far fewer moving parts. When the chips will accept 45°C (113°F) fluid, the business case for putting a mechanical refrigeration plant on the roof of a new build gets hard to defend in most climates. That is the part that has not yet fully registered outside the cooling specialists.
Getting to 45°C isn't free

Designing systems around these higher inlet temperatures still takes real engineering work – sizing the loops, choosing the dry coolers, and making sure the facility can run at the new set points without surprises. Existing buildings add another layer. Many were built with pipes, pumps, and heat exchangers sized air cooling or lower temperature liquid. Raising liquid inlet temperature means checking flow rates, pressure drops, and making sure the existing set-up delivers.

At SC26 I had meetings with a couple of companies that do this work and buttonholed more in their booths. My top-of-mind questions were: Are the 45°C (113°F) inlet temps for real? Yes, they are, and are being used as a design basis to an extent – they need to leave headroom, of course.

Any news on whether the other chipmakers are going to hit the Nvidia number on inlet temperature? Attendees were closed-lipped on this one. Nothing public from the other vendors (AMD/Intel/Arm). But on the cooling vendor side, they are happy to see the increase and will comply.

My instincts are telling me that the other chipsters may have been caught flatfooted by Nvidia's 45°C stake in the ground, but those same instincts also tell me that handfuls of Peanut M&Ms healthy snacks. I’ll nose around more.

There's real money at stake here from a TCO standpoint. One cooling vendor reports that their initial testing shows 3 percent to 4 percent cooling energy cost decrease for every additional 1°C inlet temperature increase. That's a significant number at scale.
We're approaching a point where industry advances are answering many of the objections (the real ones, not the hysterical ones) raised by the anti-data center movement.
Much lower energy use, water consumption down by 85 percent to 90 percent, higher efficiency and lower costs. Not a bad deal, right? ®

c726a5af6b120d4c: Avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.

Davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.

The hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a new way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows users to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.

Researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.
The loss of a limb

In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.

The accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, says Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.

Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”

Davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he says.

The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he says. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.
New connections

A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, says Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.

Davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.

A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”

In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” says George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.

Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, says George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.

The team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he says.
COURTESY OF AVI DAVIDSON
That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.

To get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, says George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”

The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” says George.
Becoming bionic

Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.

He’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” says Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.

At first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”

Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.
Today, he says, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.

The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Curiously, he also says he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.

The phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology company that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” says Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.

Davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he says.
George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he says. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”

Davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he says. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”

75f161629f7218ae: The Information Commission's Office (ICO) has reprimanded the UK Home Office over a border watchlist system launched without an effective way to correct inaccurate personal information.
The regulator said the failings risked people being wrongly detained for additional checks at the UK border, potentially causing distress and other harm.

The platform in question, Helios, was slated to replace its predecessor, Warnings Index, in September 2024 and despite an initial delay due to concerns over data quality, went live the following month.

Both Helios and Warnings Index are watch-listing systems, designed to allow law enforcement officials – mainly but not exclusively Border Force – to check people's data against official records at the UK border.

Helios's federated operating model, whereby the data sources are not centrally managed, yielded quicker results than Warnings Index, but contained a critical flaw in that operational staff could not alter incorrect records.

Platform operators, such as Border Force officers, could not amend the data that feeds into it, neither after the fact nor in real time. This was not the case with Warnings Index, which had a dedicated team responsible for correcting data entries in real time.
Under Helios, staff were supposed to report inaccuracies to the organization responsible for the relevant source data, which would make the correction.
One slight problem: there was no established reporting system at the time Helios was launched on October 2.
The platform went live anyway, as officials deemed the data integrity and security risks presented by Warnings Index to be greater than those of Helios.
Just nine days passed before the Home Office's data protection officer had to submit a breach report after Helios operational staff said they didn't know how to request data corrections.
During the time, Helios operators sent 87 data rectification requests to the Warnings Index correction team, despite it having no capability to make the required changes to the data.

The Home Office later said that many other requests likely weren't logged as the proper processes were not in place, and that staff should have logged the issue through a ServiceNow IT ticket, as any other departmental civil servant with any kind of IT issue would have.
But the Home Office also said that including personal data in those helpdesk tickets would itself constitute a data breach.

The ICO said in its reprimand document [PDF] that it is "unclear" how such a reporting arrangement could realistically work in practice, given that a report would require details from a subject's record that required rectification as well as the new, accurate information that should be used to replace it.

The Home Office's proposed workaround was to get operational staff to verbally read out said personal data over a phone call with the IT helpdesk – a procedure it described as possible "but cumbersome."

It took the Home Office more than a year to implement a temporary data-rectification method, which involved a BX Data Query tile on the IT Now platform, allowing Helios operators to securely report data accuracy issues.
The new method went live on October 25, 2025.
By March 18, 2026, the Home Office said the new process had received more than 6,500 correction requests and around 5,000 records had been removed.

The ICO said it "remains concerned" about the efficacy of this method, given that operators cannot include personal data in the tile report, but the regulator is satisfied the problem is at least in part fixed.
The Home Office also said it was aware of an increase in customer complaints following Helios's launch, and around 800 cases in which people were delayed at the UK border pending additional checks.
It was unable to attribute a specific number of these to Helios's technical issues, however.
"The Home Office further stated that it was not aware of any data subjects suffering distress as a result of using its services at the UK border," the ICO's report stated.
A Home Office spokesperson told us: "We take data protection extremely seriously. That is why we have co-operated fully with the Information Commissioner's Office.
"We immediately removed all outdated records to minimize delays to passenger journeys and strengthened mechanisms to speed up updates.
"Our processes will continue to be kept under review, ensuring we meet data protection obligations while protecting border security."

Joanne Stones, investigations manager at the ICO, said: "People must be able to trust that decisions about their immigration status at the UK border are made with accurate, up to date information." She added: "They also have the right to expect that when information is inaccurate, there is a swift and efficient way for it to be corrected.

"We recognize that federated systems like Helios present unique challenges and welcome the steps the Home Office has taken since this issue was identified. However, the Home Office must ensure that its permanent solution provides a robust and effective way to identify and correct inaccurate information without delay."

The ICO's public sector enforcement policy favors guidance, reprimands, and other interventions, reserving fines for the most egregious cases. Its rationale is to avoid diverting money from public services and effectively punishing those affected twice.

Fines have included £350,000 for a 2021 MoD email that exposed details of Afghan evacuation applicants, and £750,000 for the PSNI's 2023 disclosure of workforce information, including surnames, initials, ranks, and roles. The PSNI penalty was reduced from £5.6 million under the public sector approach. ®

20cd2a3f8099fed0: KUALA LUMPUR، Nov 26 — The Negeri Sembilan Palace is expected to announce its decision on the positions of the menteri besar and state executive councillors following a meeting between the state’s Ruler and senior Barisan Nasional (BN) leaders this afternoon.

Deputy Prime Minister and BN chairman Datuk Seri Ahmad Zahid Hamidi indicated that an agreement had been reached during the audience، but said the final decision rested with Yang di-Pertuan Besar Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir.
Zahid، who is also Umno president، described the meeting as having taken place in a calm atmosphere، Utusan Malaysia reported.
“We had an audience with Tuanku in a calm atmosphere، and Tuanku will make the decision.
“Let the statement from the palace finalise the decision that we have jointly agreed upon، ” he told reporters outside Istana Hinggap here today.
Zahid also indicated that the state’s political impasse could soon be resolved.
“God willing، it will be resolved soon، ” he said.
Zahid arrived at the palace at about 3pm and left approximately an hour later.

Also present were Umno deputy president and Negeri Sembilan BN chairman Datuk Seri Mohamad Hasan، BN secretary-general Datuk Seri Zambry Abd Kadir and Minister in the Prime Minister’s Department (Law and Institutional Reform) Datuk Seri Azalina Othman Said.
Earlier، Menteri Besar Datuk Ismail Lasim، who is also the Juasseh assemblyman، arrived at the palace at about 1.18pm for an audience with Tuanku Muhriz.
The meetings come amid continuing uncertainty over Ismail’s position and the functioning of the state administration.
The latest dispute arose on November 16 when Zambry announced Ismail’s purported resignation as menteri besar.

The following day، the palace clarified that Ismail remained in office، stating that under the state constitution، his resignation would only take effect upon its acceptance by the Yang di-Pertuan Besar.
On November 20، Ismail told reporters that he had neither submitted the resignation letter nor consented to its submission.

The palace also said Ismail was required to demonstrate that he retained majority support in the state legislative assembly and submit a proposed line-up of executive councillors for Tuanku Muhriz’s consideration.
Dates for the next state assembly sitting and the tabling of the 2027 state Budget would be determined once both matters had been resolved.
The state administration has been without its 10 executive councillors since their appointments were revoked by Tuanku Muhriz in September amid a dispute over the Ruler’s position.

It was previously reported that Ismail’s position was expected to be determined this week، following reports that all 24 BN and Perikatan Nasional (PN) assemblymen had lost confidence in his leadership.
242c9662f380ffeb: PUTRAJAYA, Nov 26 — Malaysia recorded an average recidivism rate of 11 per cent among former prisoners nationwide this year, reflecting the effectiveness of rehabilitation programmes implemented by the Prisons Department.
Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail said the rate was measured over a three-year period after an inmate’s release, placing Malaysia among the best-performing countries internationally.
“I am proud of this figure because we are among the best-performing countries, and I congratulate the Prisons Department on this achievement. However, I do not want them to become complacent.
“If possible, they should strive to bring the rate down to single digits,” he told reporters after attending the Home Ministry’s monthly assembly here today.
Saifuddin Nasution said the Prisons Department must continue improving its rehabilitation modules rather than rest on its achievements, to prevent former inmates from reoffending.
“These modules are not static. Through our engagement programmes with other countries, we identify good practices that may be suitable for adoption here.

“Each module is carefully designed to target rehabilitation in three aspects of human development: physical, spiritual and mental well-being. Its effectiveness is measured, among other things, through the recidivism rate,” he said.

Elaborating, Saifuddin said stigma and societal prejudice were among the factors that could drive former prisoners to reoffend, as they often struggled to gain acceptance after serving their sentences.

He said this was particularly challenging for former inmates convicted of drug-related offences, who often faced difficulties securing support from their families and communities, hindering their reintegration into society.
He urged the public to discard prejudices against former prisoners and allow them to rebuild their lives.

To support their reintegration, the Prisons Department has also established 13 halfway houses for former inmates who lack family or community support, including those who have secured employment but have nowhere to live.
Saifuddin Nasution added that about 75 per cent of the country’s prison population comprised individuals convicted of drug-related offences. — Bernama
7105da8028e99cfc: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 26 — Xiaomi reported revenue of 107.2 billion yuan (RM66.19 billion) in the third quarter and gained a larger share of the global smartphone market even as phone makers worldwide shipped 20 per cent fewer handsets than a year earlier.
In a statement yesterday, the company said its unaudited results showed an adjusted net profit of 4.9 billion yuan (RM3.03 billion) for the three months ended September 30.
Xiaomi shipped 30.7 million smartphones worldwide during the quarter.
It accounted for 12.1 per cent of global smartphone shipments, its third consecutive quarterly gain in market share, according to research firm Omdia.
In South-east Asia, Xiaomi ranked second, accounting for nearly one in every five smartphones shipped in the region.
Average phone price hits a record
Xiaomi said memory chips cost two to three times as much as they did at the start of the year, prompting it to adjust which phones it shipped and how it priced them.
The average selling price of a Xiaomi smartphone rose 39.8 per cent from a year earlier to a record 1,486 yuan (RM917.46).
Revenue from smartphones alone rose 8.2 per cent from the previous quarter to 45.6 billion yuan (RM28.15 billion).
Among the phones Xiaomi launched in September was the Xiaomi 18 Fold, a foldable model that uses one of the company’s own chips and is priced from 10,999 yuan (about RM6,791).
The wider business that includes smartphones, connected devices and internet services brought in 83.4 billion yuan (RM51.49 billion), more than three-quarters of group revenue.
Its gross profit margin was 20.4 per cent, meaning that for every 100 yuan in revenue, about 20 yuan remained after covering the direct cost of the goods and services sold.
By the end of September, more than 1.2 billion devices were connected to Xiaomi’s platform, excluding smartphones and tablets.
Cars bring in a fifth of Xiaomi’s revenue
Xiaomi’s other business segment, which includes vehicles, artificial intelligence and other new ventures, brought in 23.9 billion yuan (RM14.76 billion).
Vehicles accounted for 22.7 billion yuan (RM14.01 billion) of that total, or about a fifth of group revenue.
Xiaomi delivered 100,975 vehicles in the quarter, topping 100,000 for the second quarter in a row, and launched its SkyNomad range of SUVs in September.
4bcd8f0b1ebb6ffb: KATHMANDU, Nov 26 — Nepal has begun a process to legally declare dead thousands of people still missing after its catastrophic summer floods, authorities said Thursday, three months after the disaster.
A high-altitude glacier on the Nepal-China border collapsed on August 26, unleashing a torrent of water, ice, rock and debris.
In Nepal, the floods killed more than 1,400 people and left over 5,500 missing.
“We have started the process to declare the missing dead by verifying their details,” Ram Bahadur KC, spokesman for the disaster management authority, told AFP.
Authorities have issued public notices naming about 4,000 missing people, including 623 foreign nationals, and asked for objections or corrections before formal declarations are made.
Additional names can be added following further verification, with the government expected to issue death declarations once legal procedures are completed.
The move follows a change in Nepal’s laws last month, reducing the waiting period to declare disaster victims dead from 12 years to around six weeks.
The flood was one of the deadliest disasters in the Himalayan nation’s history.
Despite weeks of rescue operations involving hundreds of workers combing through mountains of mud and debris, only a handful of missing people were found alive.
Just 112 bodies have so far been identified and returned to their families.
The absence of death certificates has left many families unable to claim compensation, transfer property or settle other legal matters.
Some families have already held symbolic cremation ceremonies for those whose bodies have never been recovered.
In China, state media reported in September that 43 people had died and 519 were missing on the Tibetan side of the border, saying the situation was “still under further investigation”.
Beijing has not provided an update since then, and when asked by AFP on Thursday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman directed the question to the “competent authorities”. — AFP
a3a0ec5f2e3176e1: LONDON: Britain signed an £8 billion contract to upgrade its nuclear submarine facilities with Babcock on Thursday, as part of what the defence minister said was a focus on ensuring the country was "warfighting ready".

Citing the growing threat from Russia, Wes Streeting said last month that Britain needed to be ready to fight or deter military action within 1,000 days, although that mission is complicated by the country's constrained national budget.
"Our nuclear submarines are the cornerstone of our national security," Streeting said in a statement.
"Even when we have to move funding from other departments, we will prioritise our nuclear deterrent and getting Britain warfighting ready," Streeting said.
The 5-year contract with Babcock will be the single biggest procurement decision of the current parliament, Streeting said, and will ensure submarines maintenance can take place more quickly.
In recent years, Royal Navy submarines, which ensure Britain's Continuous At-Sea Deterrence policy, have had to conduct longer than usual deployments because of a lack of maintenance facilities.
The deal will create around 3,000 new highly skilled jobs, mainly across Plymouth, Clyde and Bristol with around 2,500 apprentice and graduate roles also added.
f067e2f75ccbe3a4: Donate to our Independent Journalism Spotlight issue, and get more of the coverage you value!
Originally published on Global Voices
Image made via Canva Pro. All images fair use.

Journalism has been a vital part of society for centuries. Writing about what happened and sharing it with others; reading about what happened somewhere else and discussing it with those around you; having a platform for letters, comments, and opinion about everything from the niche to the rich. Journalism has toppled governments and CEOs, revealed complicated scams, brought out the beauty of ethnographically observed daily life, recorded our qualms and foibles for posterity, and whipped up outrage, empathy, and triumph.

But journalism is on a precipice. The shift from print to digital has opened up new possibilities, as well as vulnerabilities. Changes in how we interact, especially at a distance, have changed what (and how) people want to read, listen to, or watch to understand the news.

This decade has seen dramatic changes in the field, from the loss of foundational trust in the institution, to digital, legal, and physical threats to journalists to the near-complete erosion of financial security for people who carry out this work. Increasingly authoritarian governments turn on the media, and the press in countries from Hong Kong to Myanmar to Russia to Nicaragua has been forced into exile.

Even countries such as the UK and the US have seen government targeting of journalists for critical reporting. Israel’s genocide in Gaza has laid bare the hypocrisy of the international press establishment, causing a crisis of confidence, while small local news outlets and independent journalists continue to report despite this.

Through it all, journalists have kept documenting, analyzing, responding, and reporting, even when they are underpaid and overworked, face hostile governments and terrible technology, sometimes from exile, in terrible conditions, even at risk of their lives. As we begin 2027, Global Voices will turn the spotlight onto these voices that continue to speak truth to power and bring to light the news that we all need to know. We will look at civic journalism, find out what is changing, and meet some of these indefatigable defenders of our right to free speech and our right to information.

f19b0991de69df17: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 26 — Allianz Malaysia Berhad has unveiled “Allianz Eterna,” a specialised wealth management and protection platform tailored for high-net-worth individuals, leveraging its newly established offshore subsidiary in Labuan to court the country’s surging affluent demographic.

“The wealth landscape is changing, both here in Malaysia and across the region,” Slavich said during the launch.

f5f4edeca43698aa: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia will continue negotiations with the US until the first quarter of 2027 to ensure that overall tariffs on Malaysian goods do not exceed 19%, particularly in addressing concerns over structural excess capacity and production under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, says investment, trade and industry minister Johari Ghani.

He said Malaysia would continue engaging with the US trade representative (USTR) to present its case and prevent any additional tariff measures from pushing the overall tariff rate on Malaysian goods above the 19% level agreed on under the reciprocal trade agreement (ART).
"The US indicated a tariff range of between 18% and 25% for Malaysia ... this is the range.

"But we still have until the first quarter to negotiate, explain and put forward our justification why we cannot be placed in this range. Overall, you also need to take into consideration that it cannot be more than 19%," he told reporters after the official commemoration of BYD's local assembly plant in Malaysia.

It was earlier reported that the US had proposed additional tariffs of up to 18% on Malaysian goods after determining that Malaysia’s industrial policies and manufacturing practices contributed to structural excess capacity and production that Washington said burdened or restricted US commerce.

Malaysia is among 14 economies facing proposed tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act 1974, with headline rates ranging from 15% to 35%. Other economies include China, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, Japan and the EU.
Johari said Malaysia had made its position clear to the USTR’s deputy representative, stressing that the country should retain the benefit of being among the first to sign the trade agreement.

"Look, we were the first to sign the ART, and you promised us a 19% tariff rate. We must therefore be able to enjoy that benefit. Whatever additional measures you intend to impose, including the 10% tariff related to forced labour, the total must not exceed 19%," he said.
He said the US was looking into four areas under Section 301 of the Trade Act 1974, namely excess capacity, forced labour, environmental issues and state subsidies.
He said the US had finalised a 10% tariff on forced labour while measures relating to excess capacity remained under consideration.

"On excess capacity, the US has yet to finalise its position and is still working on how to implement it. However, the investment, trade and industry ministry has consistently maintained that Malaysia does not have excess capacity," he said.
Johari said Malaysia’s position remained unchanged despite the indicative tariff range of 18% to 25% communicated by the US under its excess capacity assessment.

Meanwhile, he said the iron and steel sectors could come under scrutiny in the excess capacity investigation, particularly over concerns that production capacity could be used to channel exports through Malaysia.
However, the semiconductor sector was excluded from the assessment at this stage, he added.

429fb4d3695de462: Deprivation is behind the sharp rise highlighted in the Natsal study, and that’s an outrage. High energy bills should never be a factor in reproductive choice The National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal) is the crowdpleaser of the data world. Nerds love it because of its extraordinary thoroughness. It’s one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world, surveying nearly 7,000 people in the UK between the ages of 16 and 59, once a decade. Everyone else loves it because they get to talk about sex. Some of the statistics speak for themselves – among 25- to 34-year-old women, the number who say they never want children has gone up fourfold, a sad, completely understandable reflection of the outside world. Other figures, though, are mysterious: the number of women aged 16 to 24 who are on the pill has dropped precipitously, from nearly half to less than a third. Over the same period, the online space has been flooded with information about hormonal contraception, some of it better than it has ever been – more accessible, more accurate – and some of it plain wrong. Is there strategic, funded disinformation coming from Christian fundamentalists, such as we have already seen in the abortion space, where anti-abortion activists hose money at putatively “grassroots” online influencers? Or is it a quirk of the algorithms that once you go down the rabbit hole of “has the pill made me depressed?”, you will be shown endless influencers who have experienced that very (improbable) thing? It’s hard for a young person to navigate what’s real, and it’s hard to distinguish superstition from preference. 7dd7ac6c057431c4: SINGAPORE, Nov 26 — Nvidia has instructed its primary manufacturing partners to freeze shipments of artificial intelligence servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Indonesia, as the United States intensifies export restrictions to cut off Chinese tech firms from advanced computing power.

Original equipment manufacturers including Dell Technologies and Super Micro Computer (Supermicro), which assemble Nvidia’s graphic processors into enterprise server racks, have notified buyers across the four Southeast Asian nations that Nvidia will not permit pending hardware orders to leave factory floors, according to people familiar with the matter, Financial Times reported.

While it remains unclear whether the halt is a temporary pause as manufacturers interpret Washington’s updated compliance directives, the freeze threatens to disrupt critical technology supply chains across the region.

The four Southeast Asian nations have become prime destinations for Chinese artificial intelligence developers seeking to access Nvidia’s most advanced processors, which are barred from direct export to mainland China.

The regional trade has proved exceptionally lucrative for the Silicon Valley chipmaker, which recorded US$104 billion in revenue through its Singapore operating subsidiary in 2025, a 72 per cent surge over 12 months that also captures regional billing for Taiwan and China.

To circumvent American export curbs, numerous Chinese developers have relied on renting computing clusters from offshore cloud hosting providers that purchase server equipment powered by restricted American chips.

The US Commerce Department introduced aggressive trade rules last week designed to extinguish the practice. The clampdown followed a turbulent leadership crisis that saw Jensen Huang temporarily step down as Nvidia chief executive amid revelations of personal relationships, including with an executive linked to a Singaporean cloud company under federal investigation for semiconductor diversion.
The updated federal rules mandate a strict 90-day window for regional cloud providers to secure an export licence by verifying that their customer portfolios exclude restricted Chinese entities.

“There’s this new rule but no guidance on execution,” an executive at an affected regional cloud provider said. “No one knows how to apply for this licence while the 90-day clock is ticking. It’s causing sheer chaos in the region.”

The shipment freeze directly threatens Southeast Asia’s multi-billion-dollar data centre boom, striking heavily at Malaysia and Indonesia, where global technology companies and institutional funds have poured billions into hyperscale AI facilities.

The regulatory shock is already unravelling regional commercial deals. Singapore-based cloud firm Aolani, which had negotiated leases to supply advanced computing power to TikTok parent ByteDance, has seen commercial lenders withhold approximately US$500 million in credit facilities, pushing the arrangement towards collapse.
Despite hopes that Huang’s reinstatement this week might soften the enforcement posture, suppliers indicate that Nvidia is moving aggressively to ensure full compliance with federal directives.

Because China's leading artificial intelligence laboratories remain deeply dependent on Nvidia’s hardware to train foundational models, the regional bottleneck delivers an immediate blow to Beijing’s technology ambitions while leaving Southeast Asia's digital infrastructure sector in limbo.
Nvidia declined to comment, while Dell, Supermicro, ByteDance, and Aolani did not respond to requests for comment.

fd252bdc46a7f13a: SEOUL: South Korea's central bank hiked interest rates to a two-year high on Thursday as it fights to rein in inflation, while it also lifted its economic growth forecasts thanks to an AI-fuelled surge in exports to record highs.
The Bank of Korea's decision to lift borrowing costs 25 basis points to 3.25% marks the first increase since August and comes with inflation well above its 2% target.
The consumer price index hit 2.8% last month, with core inflation – which strips out volatile food and energy costs – the same.
Still, officials said they expected Asia's fourth-largest economy to expand 3.9% this year and 4.1% in 2027 owing to robust exports of AI-related chips.
"While tensions persist in the Middle East, the global economy is expected to maintain a solid growth trend, bolstered by robust investment in AI," the bank said.
"Meanwhile, inflation is projected to remain high for the time being as the impact of rising energy prices broadens."

South Korea – home to leading chipmakers Samsung Electronics and SK hynix – announced this month that exports had already hit US$1 trillion this year for the first time, fuelled by demand for semiconductors amid the global AI boom.
Only the United States, China and Germany have reached the milestone so far in 2026.
Governor Shin Hyun-song said semiconductor firms earned an estimated 700 trillion won (US$521.4 billion) in operating profit this year.
"About a fifth of the national income is expected to come from chipmakers' operating profit," he told reporters.

The central bank said a booming chip sector would continue to drive strong export and investment growth, while rising incomes and increased government spending were expected to support a gradual recovery in consumption.

"The future growth trajectory remains subject to uncertainties, including the extent to which the expansion in the semiconductor sector will spread to the domestic economy, as well as developments regarding the situation in the Middle East," the bank said.

The government wants that system to autonomously route complaints to relevant agencies, to automate actions like sending crews to patch up damaged roads. Critics have pointed to vague wording in the tender as potentially allowing the UP government to link this system to other agencies – a matter of concern given Indian state and national governments have implemented internet shutdowns to stop protestors from communicating on social media services and messaging apps.

Another use case is a knowledge assistant for state police that looks up case histories and other data but can’t use it to assess evidence or provide investigative conclusions. An app for teachers will advise them on how to create custom content to meet students’ needs. Healthcare workers would also get an app to help them make recommendations during patient visits.
Citizens get natural language interfaces to a system that offers advice on how to identify and access government services and schemes.
UP wants to drive these apps with self-hosted open-weight models, and to use only anonymized datasets.

India’s Internet Freedom Foundation worries that the systems described in the tender aren’t explicitly authorized by any legislation, and that the document doesn’t mention important oversight measures for the AI Stack. ®
f417bea90036f0ef: KUALA LUMPUR: KK Mart Retail Bhd, the Malaysian convenience-store chain whose first attempt at an initial public offering was delayed by a religious controversy, is launching a RM462 million (US$112 million) share sale as it prepares to add hundreds of outlets across the country.

The operator of more than 1,000 round-the-clock stores has been valued at RM1.9 billion and is set to list on Dec 15, according to a prospectus filed Thursday. The IPO comprises as many as 840 million shares priced at up to 55 sen each, including 210 million new shares and 630 million existing ones.

The listing adds to a run of Malaysian consumer companies going public after years of resilient household spending helped fuel expansion at homegrown retailers, following mini-mart operator 99 Speed Mart Retail Holdings Bhd in 2024 and dollar-store chain Eco-Shop Marketing Bhd in 2025. Malaysia’s economy has also grown faster than expected for much of 2026 despite external pressures.

KK Mart had planned to go public earlier, but the offering was postponed after socks bearing the word “Allah” were found for sale at one of its outlets in 2024, sparking a nationwide controversy and petrol-bomb attacks on several stores.

“We took a step back a little, and made sure we are truly prepared for the IPO,” founder and group managing director Chai Kee Kan, better known as KK Chai, said in an interview. “We enhanced our standard operating procedure, our supply chain, it put us in a better position.”

The group decided to proceed because going public “was always a part of our journey,” Chai said. The share sale would help fund the next stage of growth while also rewarding long-serving employees and business partners, he added.

KK Mart plans to use part of the proceeds to expand its network to 1,500 outlets by 2028 as Malaysia still has plenty of room for more convenience stores, according to Chai. Kuala Lumpur has about 14,000 people for every outlet, he said, compared with as few as 1,000 people per store in markets including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

The convenience store chain began with a single Kuala Lumpur shop in 2001 before moving into the 24-hour format. It took Chai more than a decade to reach 100 locations, but growth accelerated sharply after that.

The group says it holds more than 70% market share in Malaysia’s 24-hour convenience-store segment. That figure excludes rivals such as 7-Eleven Malaysia Holdings Bhd, which typically carries fewer household staples such as diapers, detergents, floor cleaners and toiletries. It also excludes 99 Speed Mart, which generally operates regular hours.
c33824add609296e: WASHINGTON, Nov 26 — The United States on Wednesday unveiled proposed tariffs on the European Union, China and a dozen other countries over their alleged unfair economic practices, threatening renewed tensions with both friends and foes via President Donald Trump’s trade war.
The proposal follows a months-long investigation into excess manufacturing capacity and production, launched days after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s previous slew of tariffs.
The duties range up to 20 per cent and face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January.
A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, noted that the proposals seek to take existing trade deals into account.

The new levies target some of the largest US trading partners, including China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam.
China is among the countries facing the highest 20-per cent tariff, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing.

“China understands that we’re going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding,” he told US broadcaster CNBC, adding that the US was offering China exemptions on around US$30 billion (RM123 billion) of goods.
The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected Washington to stick by a deal struck with Brussels last year.

“The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said.
China’s foreign ministry, responding to a question about the new levies before they were officially announced, warned Washington not to engage in “tariff wars and trade wars.”
Not stacked on deals
Vietnam also faces a proposed 20 per cent tariff; Cambodia and Indonesia 18 per cent; and India 17 per cent, according to the USTR’s office.
Partners like the EU, Korea and Taiwan, which have signed earlier trade deals, will see tariffs broadly capped at 15 per cent.
In a separate announcement, USTR also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.
The Brazilian president’s office called the tariffs “unacceptable” and said Brazil would “not yield to this type of threat.”

Trump’s tariffs have targeted Washington’s friends and foes alike, and are part of a push in his second term to remake global trade by forcing countries to buy US products or produce their goods in his country.
With Trump preparing to host G20 leaders in Miami next month, the senior US official rejected the notion that the new tariffs could cause tensions at the summit.
“We actually expect that we may be signing more agreements at the G20 in the wake of these announcements,” the official said.
Inflation pressures
Overcapacity concerns affect a range of sectors, from batteries to cement, chemicals to processed food, the senior US official said.
The duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now likelier to pass on expenses to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living.
Affordability was a key issue in recent US midterm elections, which saw Trump’s Republican Party swept out of power in both chambers of Congress by Democrats.
The US Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge also came in at a three-year high in October.

Fed policymakers, responsible for keeping inflation to a long-term two-percent target, say that most price effects of Trump’s previous tariff rollout have passed through the economy – but any new levies could push prices up further.
‘Hollowing out’

Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus told AFP that he expected this probe to be among “the most important” actions for the Trump administration, given its underlying concern that factories with excess capacity start operations abroad and “never get turned off, even if there’s no demand.”
This potentially leads to an oversupply of goods, depressed prices and a “hollowing out” of US manufacturing, he added.
While the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s global tariffs in February, his sector-specific duties remain intact.
The new tariffs will not stack on top of those sector-specific tariffs on items like automobiles and steel, the senior US official said.
In July, Trump imposed a separate wave of tariffs on 60 economies, accusing them of insufficient action against forced labour.
For economies facing both the forced labour and excess production tariffs, the levies would not stack, the US official said. Instead, the higher rate of the two would prevail. — AFP
cece322369c26acc: NEW DELHI: India has said that trade concerns should be addressed through ongoing talks with Washington after the US proposed raising tariffs on Indian goods to 17%.

"India and the United States are engaged in negotiations for a bilateral trade agreement," New Delhi's commerce ministry said late Wednesday, saying it was working towards an "early conclusion" of a deal.
"It has been India's position that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of these negotiations," the statement added.
The two countries reached an interim trade agreement in February aimed at reducing US tariffs on Indian goods.
However, the US Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs days later, fuelling uncertainty over when the agreement would take effect.
The two sides have been negotiating ever since.
However, on Wednesday, Washington – after a months-long probe into alleged excess production – proposed a 17% rate on India.
"India engaged constructively throughout this investigation," New Delhi added.
"In response...the department of commerce stated that India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector."
The new tariffs face a period of public comment before taking effect.
Indian finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said in October that the talks had reached "a plateau, beyond which giving or taking might be very, very difficult".
US secretary of state Marco Rubio, on a visit to India shortly after, was more upbeat, saying the two sides were "about as close as you can be without having an executed agreement".

1d227140baa5ebec: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 26 — The ringgit opened higher against the US dollar on Thursday as investors remained cautious over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, driving demand for safer assets.
At 8 am, the local currency strengthened to 4.1135/1220 against the greenback compared with yesterday’s close of 4.1170/1220.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the US dollar index (DXY) fell 0.10 per cent to 103.708 points, despite an increase in the United States’ Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) inflation rate to 3.8 per cent in October from 3.7 per cent in September.
He said the two-year and 10-year US Treasury yields also fell by four and seven basis points to 4.65 per cent and 4.86 per cent, respectively.
“The decline in US Treasury yields gives the impression that there was a flight-to-quality as markets were having doubts whether the AI boom will continue to support AI-related stock prices.
“As such, ringgit is expected to maintain its tight range trade today,” he told Bernama.
At the opening, the ringgit traded lower against a basket of major currencies.

It eased against the euro to 4.5125/5218 from 4.5036/5091 at Wednesday’s close, edged down vis-a-vis the British pound to 5.3932/4044 from 5.3756/3821, and was softer against the Japanese yen to 2.5837/5892 from 2.5820/5853.
Against its Asean peers, the ringgit traded mixed.

It inched up vis-a-vis the Indonesian rupiah to 224.4/224.9 from 224.6/224, but depreciated against the Singapore dollar to 3.1880/1951 from 3.1858/1899 and lower against the Thai baht to 12.0751/1093 from 12.0599/0798.
The local note was flat versus the Philippine peso at 6.46/6.48. — Bernama
e3565d734b25b8c7: SHANGHAI: The dollar was steady in Asian trading on Thursday after dropping to a one-week low overnight, as falling Treasury yields and fragile risk sentiment offset the greenback's usual safe-haven appeal ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.

The US dollar index slipped overnight as US equities pared losses and showed little reaction to strong economic data, leaving it well off a 19-month high struck on Monday when Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia chief executive reignited the artificial intelligence trade, while also bolstering confidence that robust US economic growth could warrant further rate hikes.
"The risk-reward of chasing further USD gains looks less attractive, but hawkish Fed risks should keep the dollar supported," said Sim Moh Siong, an FX strategist at OCBC.
He said that the dollar's relationship with equities could remain choppy, caught between safe-haven demand and concerns that a deeper AI slowdown could weigh on US growth.

The yen edged 0.1% higher against the dollar, trading around 159.06 in early Asian trade. The euro was little changed at US$1.097 as the market's focus turned to the accounts of the October European Central Bank meeting, scrutinised for hints on the rate outlook.
The US dollar index, which measures the greenback's strength against a basket of six currencies, was flat at 103.7.

Hotter-than-expected US core personal consumption expenditures inflation in October, a sharp upward revision to third-quarter gross domestic product and a Federal Reserve survey showing continued economic growth and sticky inflation cemented expectations the Fed will raise rates by 25 basis points (bps) in December and again in early 2027.

"There may also be a long weekend effect where being long bonds might not be a bad option," ING analysts said in a note. "But still, it's been a week so far in which Treasuries have ignored valid reasons for yields to rise."
Treasury yields fell across the curve, led by the long end. The 10-year yield dropped as much as 10 bps to a 2-1/2-month low of 4.8%.

Falling yields handed some relief to beaten-down currencies. The Aussie dollar recovered above 0.66 and was last at 0.6635, bouncing off an earlier low of 0.6557 that marked its weakest level in almost a year.

Adding to the sour tone, the Trump administration proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 major trading partners on Wednesday. The trade levies are meant to combat what Washington called structural excess industrial capacity, with the highest rates to hit China, which the US blames most for flooding world markets with cheap exports.
With most US markets shut on Thursday for Thanksgiving, Asia trades without fresh US price action, leaving thin liquidity for the session, market participants said.
The Swiss franc edged lower on Thursday, having firmed 0.5% overnight on safe-haven demand, while the Canadian dollar held on to a two-week high as oil prices rose.
Brent crude futures settled 3.5% higher at US$94.61 a barrel, after Yemen's Houthis said they had attacked ​Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery.
