0c810e79880a8f96: <!--kg-card-end: html--> You don’t really realize how much downtime there is in the song “Sandstorm” by Darude until you’re waiting for the bass to drop while it’s playing inside your vagina.

In August 2025, I got an email with the subject line “‘Airpods for your @ss’ raises nearly half a million in Kickstarter campaign.” I get a lot of zany pitches for products that don’t exist yet, and a lot of pitches for products that do exist but perhaps should not. This one was for a device called the Groove Thing, a sex toy that turns music into vibration patterns. But the pitch didn’t include the phrase “sex toy” at all. Instead, it’s called an “internal music player.”

I asked for a unit to review, expecting this to be purely conceptual. But they had one, and offered to send it. “The prototype functions very similarly to the final product but we do want to stress it’s a garage built prototype,” the rep for Groove Thing told me. I thought for a moment about putting something “garage built” and connected to a wall outlet into an orifice and passed. While others were braver, I decided to wait until the version they planned to send to customers in the fall was ready.

The production-ready Groove Thing arrived at my doorstep last month in an intimidatingly large box. The configuration consists of a fairly hefty speaker that’s meant to sit on your nightstand, an AC power cable, and a “resonator base,” which connects to the speaker with a pinned cord. It also came with three attachment shapes: vaginal, anal, and external (a vac-u-lock adapter is available separately for attaching your own dildos to the base). The attachment shapes are made of hard plastic, not the soft, flexible silicone I’m used to in a sex toy. They lock onto the resonator with a twist.

Opening the box and feeling the hard, inflexible plastic raised my skepticism that this thing would be comfortable. Most sex toys are covered in silky silicone that offers a little flexibility and give. But as I’m told over and over by the pamphlets that come in the box, Groove Thing “isn’t a vibrator.” Groove Thing inventor Michael Weiss-Malik, who co-founded it with Elizabeth Dell, told me it’s hard plastic for a reason, and is the result of testing feedback from the around 180 people they handed a prototype before putting it on the market.

“We started with off-the-shelf silicone dongs, and they were already producing an interesting experience for people,” Weiss-Malik told me on a call. “But we experimented with different types of materials, and what we found was that the silicone transmitted way fewer ranges of frequencies than hard plastic, and the hard plastic produces much higher fidelity.”

The mechanism that vibrates the base to the beat of the music is also different from most other sex toys on the market today, Weiss-Malik said. But he declined to share what actually runs the toy, beyond mysteriously stating it’s not “a motor.” Weiss-Malik is a former NASA engineer, where he worked on the software that helped map Mars. He’s also worked at Google, where he worked on Earth mapping software, and previously worked leadership roles at Uber and Cruise, the self-driving car company General Motors later acquired and ultimately shut down after a serious accident. But he’s been involved in the sex positive community in the San Francisco bay area “for going on 20 years,” he told me, and is the type of guy to pop into a sex shop anytime he passes one when traveling. All of this taken together makes a lot of sense to me, given that he’s also the kind of guy to spend a summer between jobs tinkering in his garage, designing a device that could put music up your ass.
Why Are Sex Toy Vibration Patterns So Terrible?
The quest for answers about how vibrator modes are tested and designed.

“Groove Thing doesn't use a motor. We don't say what is in there, but it's not a motor,” he said. “It uses a different set of physics that's more similar to audio equipment, and as a result, it can actually reproduce a full sound form, not just an on-off. You know, a sound-responsive vibrator is mostly just an on-off switch that's connecting to the beat.” Other vibrating sex toys work in that way: An eccentric rotating mass motor spins, turning pre-programmed patterns into vibration. Handheld sex toy makers have to work around several factors, including the limits of these motors, the tendency of soft silicone to dampen vibration, and the shapes they need to compact them into to fit in a device that doesn’t wear out customers’ wrists. Groove Thing seems to get around some of these problems by skipping the typical rotating motor, shaping the attachments in such a way that you can insert them and then go mostly hands-free when lying down, and choosing a plastic that feels kind of awkward at first.

The combination means different instruments and ranges come through as different levels of vibration. “A piano or bass guitar feels different than a drum kit. It almost feels like having a third ear,” Weiss-Malik said. “There's a level of fidelity there, where you have a whole new dimension to the sound that you're hearing. It works particularly well in bass, but it works all the way up to the mid frequencies.” Groove Thing replicates frequencies you can’t hear with your ears, he said — kind of like being at a concert and standing close enough to the stack that you feel it in your chest. As someone who recently almost lost their eyebrows and gained tinnitus at a Mogwai show, I get it, and I think for most people this comparison is what will make the Groove Thing click for them.

”Some of what you're feeling is subsonic; it's down below 20 hertz, and we actually reproduce that as well,” Weiss-Malik said. “So you actually experience parts of your music that you never even noticed were there before, or that your ears can't hear, and that at the very least, home stereo equipment has a very hard time reproducing. So you're getting an experience that hundreds of thousands of dollars worth of speakers are normally required for you to get that out of the recording.” This was my experience with “Sandstorm.” You wouldn’t believe how much not-music is going on in that song, but also, how the moments that seem like they should be intense rumbly bass-drops are actually at a higher register.

The creators of Groove Thing want you to be able to play whatever you want, which you can from your phone via Bluetooth or the optional aux jack, but they also really, really want you to try their intro playlist, I assume to prevent people like myself from putting “Crab Rave” on the stereo and then writing it off as a bust. That playlist is eclectic, beginning with “Beads on the Wind: The Human Experience Remix” and “Aya,” which I would place in a repeat-Burning-Man-attendee genre (no judgement here), but continues into “Blinding Lights” by The Weeknd and, to my pleasant surprise, an underrated track from Taylor Swift’s Lover album, “I Think He Knows.” An additional playlist with more songs features mostly EDM but also throws “Piece of Me” by Britney Spears in there.

This entire test run of this not-vibrator made me, an admittedly tone deaf and musically unsophisticated person (see the previous lines), realize how much is happening in music that I’m never picking up with my own two ears. The “third ear” analogy is pretty spot-on: To enjoy the Groove Thing with an open mind, you have to let go of the typical expectations of other sex tech. Climax isn’t the point. The point is to use your junk to go on a musical journey, which is something that will resonate strongly for some, and miss others.

“You know, people don’t go to a concert just to hear the finale and go home. Groove Thing isn’t a tool like most vibrators are,” Weiss-Malik told me. “It's more like a concert experience. You get to bask in pleasure for a period of time. In our early beta tester groups, most people who had unlimited usage of it used it for over an hour in their first session. Most of the second time users in that beta group also used it for over an hour in their second session.”

The entire sex tech market has been trending away from the literal, anatomical, and climax-centered for years, with more toys coming in abstracted colors, shapes, and features that focus on pleasure and experience over getting your own personal money shot. I see Groove Thing as a logical step in that evolution.
Groove Thing is shipping out orders as of this month, and retails at $369 for the single unit and more for add-ons and additional units for partnered play.
5a3b624c2bc565c0: Consumer spending has stayed healthy in large part because Americans are staying employed, whether through formal or gig work. AP Photo/David ZalubowskiHoliday shopping season is kicking off, inundating consumers with Black Friday offers. With inflation fatigue, declining real wages and stock market turbulence thrown into the mix, is the U.S. consumer on the verge of scaling back? This question has long puzzled economists, who wonder why spending has held up even as consumer sentiment slumps. As a researcher of supply chains who has also worked for years at consumer products companies, I’ve run my own studies and have been surprised, time and again, by how spending has continued at a healthy clip even when the economy is faltering. Most recently, in March 2026, I built a model to assess how the Iran war could affect global supply chains at three, six and nine months out. In the case of consumer behavior, the hit was less than what was expected. Even though Americans were paying substantially more at the gas pump due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as dealing with tariff-induced inflation and high interest rates, consumer spending held up remarkably well. I now believe I missed two things: resilience and innovation. More specifically, Americans are continuing to work, whether in formal or gig jobs, and that’s the main factor holding up spending. And as long as consumers have income, they’ll keep finding a way. What’s changing, though, is that this balancing act is getting harder for many people to keep up. What resilience looks like Resilience and innovation may sound admirable, but in practice they’re often difficult and onerous. Under “innovation,” some traditional adjustments for consumers include buying cheaper “private label” or store brands, shopping at off-brand and discount stores, or relentlessly hunting for deals. Other adjustments include eating more meals at home rather than going out, or downsizing vacation plans. “Resilience,” meanwhile, can mean taking on extra work. Economists call this the added worker effect, and it shows up during tough times. During the 2007-09 Great Recession, for example, more married women joined the labor force as unemployment rose among their spouses. In 2026, there’s an uptick in retirees heading back to work as well as an increase in the share of mothers with children who are staying in or reentering the workforce. These are both responses to the rising cost of living. More broadly, Americans are using traditional and nontraditional means to make some extra cash. About 1 in 3 workers has had a side hustle in 2026, according to the jobs database ZipRecruiter – whether it’s nanny jobs, side gigs on Etsy, delivering meals for DoorDash or driving customers for Uber. For many Americans, this work is a necessity, not just a way to earn extra discretionary cash. The increasing need for extra work over the past five years underscores the drop in purchasing power from the salaries many people earn. More Americans, including retirees in need of extra income, are taking up gig work, like driving for Uber. AP Photo/Emily Wang Fujiyama Another form of resilience can be seen through volunteering and charitable giving. In my own neighborhood, a food bank that started during the COVID-19 pandemic has helped many in the community over the past five years. Across the country, food bank donations and charitable giving continue to rise despite economic challenges. According to Giving USA, charitable giving rose to US$617 billion in 2025, surpassing the $600 billion mark for the first time. This increase addresses a growing need for food banks to feed Americans who can’t afford basic groceries anymore. At the same time, the actual number of donors is dropping. Shoppers are hitting the limit Many consumers are now running out of levers to pull. Wealthier Americans are continuing to spend at a strong clip, which is why official consumer spending data suggests the economy is steady. But it’s a different picture for the rest. One in four families are spending more than they make, as seen by rising credit delinquency and auto repossessions, according to the Atlanta Federal Reserve. Whether it’s food, healthcare, rent or cars, Americans are spending a much larger share of their income on necessities than they did 10 years ago. For especially strapped Americans, like those facing the double whammy of a car payment and a student loan, these trade-offs are especially challenging. A good example are auto loan delinquencies, now near a 10-year high. Losing a car can mean losing a job, with devastating financial consequences. Frontline workers also miss more shifts as gas prices rise. And this gets to a core lesson for understanding today’s economy: The bedrock for consumer spending remains employment. The stable job market we see right now – with unemployment at 4.1% – is critical. If this healthy job market holds and interest rates and energy prices ultimately ease, the average consumer will still tread water. But if inflation continues to run hotter than the Federal Reserve would like, and rates rise, Americans’ disposable income will likely shrink – and hurt economic growth in the process. That could lead to a domino effect: Unemployment rises, reducing the discretionary spending that had been keeping economic growth steady. Whether it comes to this, it’s important to remember that the holiday season isn’t necessarily an accurate forward-looking indicator. Shoppers often go to great lengths to make family and friends happy. The big challenge for consumers will start in early 2027. Will the Fed hike rates? Will inflation stay high? Will gas prices come down? Until these questions are answered, we’re in the “bend but don’t break” phase. Many consumers are facing challenging times in 2026, but their resilience has been a surprise on the upside. I’d like to be surprised again in 2027 – but that’s far from a sure thing. Chris Gaffney has received funding from the U.S. Department of Commerce's Economic Development Administration.
e6ea2d749ddbc7d9: Win4Wine is one of the more remarkable and creative hacks we've read about in recent years. It runs Windows XP's genuine Explorer shell through patched Wine on Debian 13, with a custom window manager integrating Linux applications into the desktop.
As its GitHub repository explains: "The taskbar, Start menu, desktop and folder windows are XP's real ones, and Linux applications get XP's frames and taskbar buttons."

This impressive, possibly demented project has English installation instructions and a README, although its design documents are in Japanese. We found Mozilla's built-in translation handled those pretty well.
Its developer goes by miKuta0407 on GitHub, their homepage, and X.

Also note, you're going to need some Windows installation media for the full experience. The README says: "No Microsoft files are included. Only the files that are needed are extracted locally from your own ISO."

It supports Windows XP Professional SP3 installation images in 32-bit Japanese or English editions, with an experimental option for Windows 7 SP1 x64. Without either Windows image, it can download and use ReactOS's free software shell instead, for what it terms "a Windows 2000-like classic look." In our view, that sounds much better anyway.

Before any former Windows users cry hurray and reach for an optical drive, this is not some ready-to-run project. The top of the README warns: "This is a personal, experimental project, not a finished product for daily use." The developer has tested it only on a fresh Debian 13 installation and recommends a VM or spare machine, rather than an existing working desktop, which sounds like an excellent precaution to us.
Also, before you ask, yes, it was vibe-coded with Claude.

We found ourselves reminded of another crazy-but-is-it project that we wrote about back in January: What if Linux ran Windows... and meant it? Meet Loss32. The Loss32 proposal was even more extreme. It suggested replacing essentially the entire Linux userland, so it would be a Linux kernel running Wine with a Windows desktop and Windows apps.

However, Mikuta-san was way ahead of us – lower down, the README mentions and even links to Loss32. Saying that, since it launched at the end of 2025, the bottom of the Loss32 web page shows a couple of updates, reporting on delays in getting it working. That, to be honest, did not shock us, but we still admire the let's-do-this spirit. The developer also seems to have got slightly distracted by a previous project, touchHLE: high-level emulator for early iOS apps.

Loss32, in turn, reminded us of Neptune OS, an attempt to give seL4 a Windows personality transplant. We wrote about that back in 2022, and work on it has continued: the project page shows updates in recent months. The team has also pushed out preview releases in 2022, 2024, 2025, and most recently in September.

This OS face transplant also reminded us of our article, Classic 7 is Windows 10 LTSC cosplaying as Windows 7. Some people really miss the look and feel of vintage Windows. Can someone do Windows NT 4 next, please? ®
79a22f2e5650c7d0: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
AI is straining America’s open records systems

AI has intensified investors’ interest in public records. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests. That could potentially make public offices less transparent.

47a9e4632e45bc05: Recovery windows of up to ten years are now available in Microsoft 365 Backup for OneDrive and SharePoint, up from a previous maximum of two.
The change took effect on October 31, though Exchange remains capped at two years.

Administrators can select recovery windows of three months, six months, or any whole number of years from one to ten. Microsoft's list price is $0.15 per GiB per month of protected content. Extended windows can increase costs by keeping deleted data billable for longer.
Switching to a longer recovery window will also not make backups for that period magically available. So no nostalgic trips back to 2016.

Wider recovery windows may appeal to organizations that need access to older data, but backups are not a substitute for compliance retention and archiving. Recovery after a breach or ransomware attack is also critical, particularly getting back to a healthy state before any malware seeped into files.
Microsoft says backups are physically redundant and geographically replicated while respecting the tenant's data residency requirements.
Full OneDrive account and SharePoint site restores offer recovery points every ten minutes for the most recent two weeks, then weekly points through the configured window, up to ten years.
Individual file and folder recovery is limited to recovery points from the most recent 14 days, regardless of the configured window.
Restore remains free, which is handy since regular testing is a vital part of any disaster recovery plan.

The arrival of a ten-year recovery window is good for enterprises that need it and have deep enough pockets. However, it is important to keep in mind that being able to configure a longer recovery window doesn't constitute a disaster recovery plan in itself and may be overkill in many instances.
Microsoft notes: "The existing one-year default recovery window remains unchanged. Longer recovery windows must be configured on the applicable backup policies."
The company also recommends that users "review your organization's SharePoint and OneDrive backup requirements to determine whether longer recovery windows are needed."
A decade of recovery history could be valuable. It also means a decade of data to account for when setting budgets, access controls, and retention policies. ®

f5bb5e8a9ad3e428: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics.

LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online.

The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI.

AutoPay lets drivers register their vehicle and payment details in advance so drop-off charges are collected automatically.
Gatwick told us it was unable to provide details about how many customers were affected by the breach, or how far back the affected records go.

The email said most affected customers would have only some of the listed data exposed. The could include names, home addresses, cities, postcodes, contact details, and AutoPay login credentials such as email addresses and bcrypt-hashed passwords were affected.
Other records implicated in the breach include details of vehicles linked to AutoPay accounts, those vehicles' entry and exit times at Times24-managed parking locations, and vehicle registrations.

Again, in a minority of cases, "some limited emails between the customer service team and customers" were also exposed, the email stated.

Airport officials are overseeing the response with outside cybersecurity specialists. Gatwick warned of possible disruption to its website but said flights were unaffected.
Customers can still use Gatwick's drop-off zones, although they'll have to use alternative payment methods, and all other airport services are still operating as usual.
The notification email urged customers to exercise caution when receiving communications from Gatwick, Times24, AutoPay, or ParkPark, especially those that ask for payment or bank details.
Times24, which operates across more than 200 car parks in the UK, did not immediately respond to our request for more information.
Dray Agha, senior manager at Huntress's tactical response division, warned that criminals could use the data for convincing scams long after news coverage of the breach has faded.

"The real damage often comes after the breach," he said. "Criminals rarely use stolen data straight away; they'll wait until the headlines fade, then send a text about a 'parking fine' or an email offering a 'refund' that references a real booking. b0deea04c96bb290: In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.
Transparency, monetized

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.

Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.

The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.
The AI detection problem

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”

As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”
Everything’s on the table

Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”

Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”
afccdcb010158c67: If courts were fast and fair, nobody would need a viral post to go home
Originally published on Global Voices
Court of Appeal building in Lagos, Nigeria. Image by King ChristLike via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

This post by Fatima Zahra Yahaya is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In February 2025, a letter from a jailed man named Thomas Jonathan Biodun reached the public after some Nigerian Twitter influencers visited his prison to play a friendly football match with the inmates. Biodun was in jail over a debt of NGN 1,137,000 (USD 758). In the letter, he said he had asked for help online before, but someone had called him a scammer.

One of the influencers shared the letter on social media. Another influencer, Sir Dickson, who goes by the handle Wizarab10 on X, pushed it further, garnering over 2.5 million views in one post. In his post, Sir Dickson said, “Nobody should be in prison over a debt. It is not a criminal offense. I have spoken to @egi_nupe [another X influencer and lawyer], and we will be taking it up. Imagine rotting in prison because you’re poor.” A public donation campaign followed, and within weeks, it had raised enough money to clear the debt.
Punch Newspapers reported that Biodun walked out of Apapa Kirikiri Correctional Center and thanked everyone who helped.
Biodun’s story has a happy ending. But it raises a hard question: Should a person’s freedom depend on the benevolence of internet strangers and how many people share a post?
The problem behind this story

In February 2026, the Nigerian Correctional Service said that most people in its custody were still waiting for trial. Many of them have not been found guilty of any crime but remain in pre-trial detention. While some of them cannot pay bail, others cannot pay court fines. In Nigeria, the crime of being poor can land you in a jail cell.

Waiting is not a small thing. While a case drags on, a person may lose their job, business, or place to live. A family can lose its breadwinner, which can derail a whole family — or even a whole community’s livelihoods.
When the internet steps in
Jonathan Biodun is not the only person who turned to the internet to seek support for injustice.

Quadri Alabi, 17, went viral in 2023 when he stood in front of former Anambra State Governor Peter Obi’s campaign convoy. He spent months in Kirikiri Prison over a robbery charge that his lawyer, Inibehe Effiong, called baseless. Effiong also said the police recorded him under the wrong age, meaning he was charged and sentenced as an adult. On April 17, 2025, he was freed. The same day, Effiong asked the public on X to help his family move to a safer home, because they were still getting threats. The International Center for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) reported that more than NGN 3 million (over USD 21,965) was raised within two hours.

Emeka Nzeruike was arrested in 2015, when he was only 12 years old, over an alleged theft. He spent 10 years in prison waiting for trial. In July 2025, a lawyer named Alexander Nzeadi, who posts on X as @_youfoundalex, took up his case, and Emeka walked out of court.

The lawyer wrote that Emeka had been alone, afraid, and forgotten, with no trial and no lawyer. He then asked Nigerians to help Emeka heal, learn a skill, and start his life again now that he was finally free. The post was seen millions of times.
The other side of the story

Look closely at these cases. Biodun, Alabi, and Nzeruike were helped because their stories reached the right people. A letter found the right hands. A lawyer or a kind stranger posted at the right time.
Biodun said he was first called a scammer. That shows how difficult it can be to be believed online.
But what about the person nobody posts about? Not every inmate has a famous friend, a lawyer, or a loud voice to advocate on their behalf. For them, it can feel like no one is watching.
This is the worry. If help comes only to the stories that go viral, then luck decides who goes home. A sad story with a clear photo may win hearts, while a quiet case may be missed.
Raising money to pay for inmates’ legal fees or fines is not new, and it is not only done online.

In 2023, The Conclave reported that public-spirited people and a group called Prisoners Rehabilitation and Welfare Action (PRAWA), a non-governmental organization (NGO), paid fines to free 37 inmates from Kuje and Suleja prisons. The Interior Minister at the time had urged Nigerians to pay the fines of some prisoners to ease crowding in prisons.
Kindness is good. But justice should not depend on luck or others’ generosity.
A hope for smart leaders

I do not believe we should stop being kind. I believe we should fix the courts, so that kindness is not the only hope a poor person has. If courts were fast and fair, nobody would need a viral post to go home.
Social media is already doing one useful thing. It shows us real faces and real stories where the system is failing. Smart leaders, lawyers, and judges can listen, and they can fix it.
Until then, every shared post is a sign that Nigerians care. It is also a sign that the courts must do better. Everyone in Nigeria deserves a fair day in court.
Written by Guest Contributor

a65f509715b5b41f: Patrick T. Fallon/GettyIt’s hard to think of Nvidia without picturing Jensen Huang. Rarely seen without his signature black leather jacket, Huang has led chipmaker Nvidia since co-founding it in 1993, turning it into a central player in the artificial intelligence (AI) boom. Earlier this month, Huang resigned as president, chief executive officer and a member of Nvidia’s board, in the wake of a bombshell scandal involving affairs and alleged corporate espionage. Days later, the board linked his departure to “personal behavior inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”. It said it did “not intend to reinstate” him. This week, however, it voted unanimously to bring him back, following a remarkable intervention by US President Donald Trump. Many analysts have already weighed in on why the US government intervened. But there’s a deeper, more fundamental question here about corporate power. If a chief executive is seen as too valuable to lose, can a company’s board still hold them to account? If it can’t, what exactly is the board for? Read more: Trump had 4 reasons to ‘convince’ Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang. Here’s why it matters globally The ‘key person risk’ Sometimes, the “hero” leader of a company can become its biggest vulnerability. In corporate governance, this is called “key person risk”. It is the danger a company comes to depend so heavily on one person that losing them would do serious damage. This problem often grows out of success. A founder who builds a business and shapes its culture becomes its public face. Staff, customers and investors start to see the person and the company as one. Think of Steve Jobs, co-founder and longtime chief executive of Apple, or even the fictional media magnate Logan Roy in the TV series Succession. Nvidia itself recognised this risk before Huang’s brief removal. Its 2026 annual report warned the company was “highly dependent on the services” of its longstanding executive team, and that failing “to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions” could hinder its success in the long term. Despite this, when Huang left, no permanent successor was ready. Nvidia’s chief financial officer, Colette Kress, stepped in temporarily while the board searched for a replacement. Who’s watching the boss? So, what is a board actually for? Shareholders can’t supervise the managers in a large company like Nvidia; instead, they elect a board of directors to do it for them. While the board isn’t involved in daily operations of the company, it approves big decisions, watches the chief executive and, if needed, replaces them. It’s designed to solve something economists call the “principal-agent problem”. A company’s managers (the agents) may put their own interests ahead of the owners’ (the principals). That’s why independence matters. Independent directors don’t work for the company and have no close financial or personal ties to its management. Filling a board with the chief executive’s employees (such as other senior executives) and friends is like letting students mark their own exams. Nvidia’s U-turn shows how fragile independence can be. A committee of independent directors is still investigating claims that Huang was targeted by China’s top spy agency. Huang is also due to answer questions from US lawmakers behind closed doors on December 1. The board brought him back before either had finished. The board acknowledged that its decision to rehire Huang was heavily influenced by the US government. It said it was “confident” Huang posed “no national security risk”, based on “input from senior US government levels”. We have seen other boards cave under pressure before. In November 2023, OpenAI’s board fired its chief executive, Sam Altman. Within days, nearly all of its 770 staff threatened to quit. Altman returned, and the board that sacked him was replaced. Independent of whom? On paper, there are strong safeguards to protect board independence. For example, the Nasdaq stock exchange, where Nvidia is listed, requires most directors to be independent. The committees that check a company’s accounts and set executive pay must be fully independent. But these rules fall short in three ways. First, the board itself gets to decide who counts as “independent”. In 2024, a US court found several Tesla directors who approved Elon Musk’s pay deal were too close to him to be independent. A higher court later restored the deal on other grounds. Second, directors get much of their information from the very executive team they are meant to be keeping in check. And third, a board without its own independent leader often struggles to push back against a chief executive. Nvidia only appointed its first-ever board chair on the day Huang resigned. Why no one should be irreplaceable “Key person” risk can’t be removed, but it can be managed. Boards can train a credible successor, appoint an independent chair before a crisis hits, and finish investigations before deciding. They should also explain their reasoning in public. An independent board that isn’t able to fire and replace a chief executive is just a cheer squad – not the umpire it’s supposed to be. This matters well beyond Silicon Valley. Many retirement funds around the world own shares in Nvidia. For the sake of protecting millions of people’s long-term savings, retirement funds and others representing shareholders should be advocating for better governance than we’ve seen at Nvidia so far. ec7b63860efa33d3: Malaysia Athletics cannot claim to have put its house in order while Karim Ibrahim remains president of one of its affiliates despite his disqualification by World Athletics.
Karim is not only the former president of Malaysia Athletics. He also heads Perak Athletics Association (Perak AA), a member of the national body.
MA’s endorsed constitution appears clear on the eligibility of people in such positions.

Article 13.2.8 bars anyone disqualified, removed or suspended by MA, the Olympic Council of Malaysia, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics or another local or international sports authority from being nominated, elected, appointed or holding office as an affiliate’s office-bearer, council member or committee member.
That restriction remains until the relevant authority lifts the sanction or the person succeeds in an appeal.

World Athletics has disqualified Karim. He has not appealed, and the sanction remains in force. The provision expressly covers office-holders in MA’s affiliates, not just those serving on its national executive council.

His position in Perak AA therefore puts MA’s responsibility to enforce its own constitution squarely in focus. The national body cannot leave the state association to decide whether it wishes to observe a rule that binds its members.
Affiliation carries obligations
MA’s authority to demand compliance rests on more than the eligibility provision.

Article 18.3 gives its constitution and by-laws precedence when they conflict with those of its members. Article 18.4 requires MA, its affiliates and people holding positions under its rules to comply with Malaysian law and the regulations of OCM, the Asian Athletics Association, World Athletics and other relevant international sports bodies.
Together, these clauses establish the obligations that come with membership. A state association cannot claim the benefits of affiliation while disregarding the rules governing the sport.
There is, however, a difference between requiring an affiliate to comply with MA’s constitution and automatically rewriting its registered rules.
If Perak AA’s constitution conflicts with the national one, it may still have to follow its own amendment procedures and the requirements of Malaysian law.

That does not excuse inaction. MA should formally notify Perak AA of the eligibility provision, explain its application and require the state body to address the position of its office-holders in accordance with the rules.

The same scrutiny should extend to every affiliate. MA must identify conflicting provisions or practices in state associations and set out what they need to do to comply. It should not wait for another dispute to expose weaknesses in its governance.
The council must be prepared to act
The executive council has a clear role in this process.

Article 18.1 gives it sole authority to interpret MA’s constitution and by-laws. Article 16.2 provides a mechanism for disputes between MA and its members, or between members. The council may seek OCM’s advice before making its final decision by majority.
These provisions give the council a way to resolve disagreements. They also place responsibility on it to address non-compliance.

That does not give the council licence to impose whatever penalty it chooses. It must identify the relevant breach, follow the proper procedures and give the affiliate a fair opportunity to respond. Any action must also comply with Malaysian law.
But procedural requirements should guide enforcement, not become an excuse to avoid it.

In Perak AA’s case, the council should establish the facts, determine the application of Article 13.2.8 and set out the steps needed to bring the state body into compliance. If Perak AA disputes the interpretation, the constitution provides a route to resolve the matter.

The same standards must apply to every affiliate. Perak AA should not receive special treatment because Karim once led the national association. Nor should any state body enjoy an exemption because of its influence or leadership.

This is not about stripping state associations of their autonomy. They should remain free to run their programmes, develop athletes and manage their affairs. But autonomy does not mean freedom to disregard the rules of the national and international sport.
The Karim episode exposed the consequences of a national body allowing its own rules to fall short of international requirements. MA must not allow that failure to continue at state level.
Its constitution gives it the authority to demand compliance. The executive council must now show that it has the resolve to use it.

Maka terpaksalah saya mencari orang yang orang Melayu hormat lebih daripada orang kerdil dalam politik seperti saya untuk memberi kesedaran tentang bahaya parti yang menunggang agama demi kuasa.

Baru-baru ini kita membaca tentang seorang pemimpin PAS yang mengatakan pemberian derma untuk membayar denda RM50 juta yang dikenakan ke atas seseorang yang didapati bersalah dalam kes penyelewengan dana adalah perbuatan yang dapat pahala. Sebelum ini, rasanya tahun lepas, PAS menjayakan tabung jihad untuk membayar saman fitnah untuk seorang wakil rakyatnya. Kedua-dua kes penyelewengan dana dan fitnah ini boleh kita telusur tanpa was-was. Kemudian, kita dapat tahu bahawa orang yang memfitnah serta orang yang pecah amanah dan salah guna kedudukan tidak menyatakan penyesalan, jauh lagi berikrar tidak akan mengulang lagi perbuatan.

Tidak cukup dengan itu, kita juga mendengar PAS menggunakan istilah munafik semasa membahaskan Belanjawan 2027 yang dibentangkan perdana menteri baru-baru ini. Ada pula presiden PAS menyifatkan Perjanjian Keyakinan dan Perbekalan yang ditandatangani antara kerajaan dan beberapa Ahli Parlimen pembangkang sebagai pendekatan dajal. Kita sudah pun maklum tentang peristiwa membaca doa qunut nazilah terhadap orang yang tidak sehaluan dengan PAS. Isu mengkafirkan orang sudah pun tercatat dalam sejarah negara.
Maka itu saya menyingkap dua ucapan Mahathir dalam Perhimpunan Agung Umno pada 1984 dan 1999. Dalam ucapan 1984, Mahathir mengecam PAS seperti berikut;

"Umno adalah parti politik orang Melayu. Oleh kerana orang Melayu semuanya beragama Islam, maka Umno dengan sendirinya menjadi parti orang Islam Semenanjung Malaysia dan berjuang untuk agama Islam. Tetapi Umno bukan hipokrit dan berpura-pura menafikan yang ia adalah parti orang Melayu seperti yang dibuat oleh sebuah parti lain.

"Umno dengan jelas mengakui yang ianya parti kebangsaan Melayu di samping menjadi parti Islam. Menafi hakikat ini akan menjadikannya hipokrit atau munafik -- dan orang munafik tidak menjadi orang Islam yang jujur.

"Tidak ada cara yang lebih berkesan untuk mengekalkan kelemahan orang Melayu daripada menggunakan orang Melayu sendiri untuk melawan orang Melayu. Dengan tertubuhnya PAS maka terbentuklah alat utama musuh orang Melayu. Malang bagi mereka, kebanyakan daripada orang Melayu dapat meneka strategi pecah-belah ini dan telah terus menyokong Umno.

"Sekarang ini usaha ditumpukan kepada melemahkan semangat kebangsaan Melayu dengan mendakwa Islam menentang kebangsaan. Bahawa kebangsaan orang Melayu adalah satu alat mempertahankan diri bagi orang Melayu yang semuanya Islam, sama seperti kebangsaan Mujahidin mempertahankan orang Islam Afghanistan, dan tidak menjadi satu keangkuhan yang mengenepikan agama Islam dan orang Islam lain, tidak disebut. Mereka yang mendakwa bahawa mereka cuma mengakui keislaman mereka dan kononnya menolak semangat kebangsaan Melayu, tidak pula berani mempertahankan orang yang seagama dengan mereka di Afghanistan, atau di Lubnan atau di lain-lain tempat. Keislaman mereka terhad kepada kegiatan di Malaysia sahaja di mana kebangsaan Melayu Umno dapat memberi perlindungan kepada mereka. Sifat mereka ini adalah sifat hipokrit atau sifat talam dua muka. Dan mereka adalah begitu fanatik kepada parti mereka sehingga mereka tidak menyoal sama ada pendirian parti mereka baik atau tidak. Mereka inilah yang sebenarnya dari golongan asabiyah."
Jelas siapa sebenarnya hipokrit yang dimaksudkan Mahathir ketika itu. Namun demikian kita dapat merasai kesamaan mesej tersebut dalam tindak tanduk PAS ketika ini.

Dalam petikan kedua ucapan yang sama, Mahathir mempertikaikan PAS bahawa mereka sahaja yang tahu Islam manakala orang lain seperti Umno ketika itu yang juga mempunyai barisan pemimpin seperti Anwar Ibrahim tidak mencerminkan Islam sebenar.

"Sebagai satu lagi usaha untuk menentukan kejayaan orang Melayu, kita telah berusaha menerapkan nilai-nilai Islam. Kita tidak syak bahawa nilai-nilai Islam akan menjadikan orang Melayu orang yang lebih berjaya di dunia dan di akhirat. Pentadbiran yang diasaskan kepada nilai-nilai Islam tetap akan menjadi pentadbiran yang kukuh, adil dan berjaya.

"Di sini nilai-nilai Islam tidak bermakna rupa bentuk dan kebudayaan Arab yang menjadi tumpuan setengah-setengah orang Melayu di Malaysia. Memang benar rupa-bentuk boleh dijadikan simbol Islam dan ditiru dengan mudah. Tetapi rupa-bentuk tidak akan membawa kejayaan kepada kita. Yang akan membawa kejayaan ialah amalan nilai-nilai Islam seperti amanah, disiplin, taat setia, rajin dan tekun, bersaudara antara orang-orang mukmin, berani kerana benar, bertoleransi dan bertimbang rasa, adil, insaf dan syukur dan lain-lain lagi nilai yang mulia yang tidak begitu mudah diamal atau dipamerkan.

"Dalam ucapan saya di perhimpunan agung 1982, saya telah menjelaskan tentang hasrat kerajaan untuk menerapkan nilai-nilai Islam ke dalam pentadbiran negara. Maksud saya ialah supaya kita akan mentadbir dengan amanah, jujur, disiplin, setia, bertanggungjawab, cekap, bersih, dan lain-lain lagi nilai Islam yang akan menjadikan pentadbiran negara ini satu pentadbiran yang berkesan dan adil.

"Malangnya hasrat ini telah dijadikan alasan untuk ajaran dan tindakan yang membawa masalah dan mengganggu pentadbiran. Islam sengaja digambarkan oleh kumpulan-kumpulan tertentu sebagai agama yang tidak toleran, sehingga kakitangan kerajaan yang beragama Islam dilarang dari berkawan dengan yang bukan Islam dan melawat mereka di hari kebesaran mereka. Tumpuan diberikan bukan kepada soal khidmat yang baik dan pegangan kepada janji dan ikrar, tetapi kepada soal haram-halal, di mana tafsiran dibuat mengikut nafsu.

"Demikianlah ekstremnya tafsiran yang dibuat sehingga ada pegawai yang tidak mahu menyentuh kertas yang ada tertulis di dalamnya perkataan 'babi'. Ada yang sanggup menukar arahan ketua kerana tidak secocok dengan fahaman ekstrim mereka. Ada yang berpendapat bahawa penerapan nilai Islam bermakna memakai cador, tetapi kerana gaji, mereka masih sanggup bekerja di pejabat."

Dalam petikan ucapan 1999 sewaktu era reformasi dan Mahathir berseteru dengan Anwar, beliau juga menyerang PAS yang bekerjasama dengan DAP. Di sini Mahathir menyebut bahawa PAS adalah parti yang boleh mengubah haluan mengikut citarasa sendiri dan memfatwakan apa saja bagi niat politik kuasa;

"PAS adalah sebuah parti yang mudah menukar haluan mengikut kepentingan semasa. Demikian pada mulanya PAS mendakwa bahawa orang Islam yang bekerjasama dengan orang bukan Islam menjadi kafir dan dengan itu PAS menolak kerjasama dengan bukan Islam. Kemudian PAS menyertai Barisan Nasional dan bekerjasama dengan orang bukan Islam dalam BN. Pada masa itu PAS tidak lagi mendakwa bahawa orang Islam yang bekerjasama dengan bukan Islam menjadi kafir. Ternampak jelas tafsiran agama oleh PAS boleh ditukar untuk kepentingan semasa.

"Kemudian PAS keluar daripada BN dan menganggap orang Umno tidak Islam sehingga ahli dan pemimpin PAS sanggup sembahyang berasingan di masjid yang sama dan membina masjid lain bagi orang PAS. Tetapi apabila pilihan raya hampir tiba, PAS mengadakan pakatan dengan DAP yang bukan Islam. Bagi PAS, orang Umno yang Islam tidak boleh dijadikan sahabat seperti PAS bersahabat dengan orang bukan Islam dalam DAP."
Kini kita melihat kebenaran kata-kata Mahathir itu apabila PAS menghumban Bersatu dan memeluk Umno serta kini memperjuangkan nasib Najib.
Akhir sekali Mahathir menyinggung isu PAS yang suka merendahkan umat Islam lain dan menampakkan diri mereka seperti orang Islam terpilih dan special dalam ungkapan seperti di bawah;

"Hari ini kita lihat kesan daripada kesanggupan PAS bekerjasama dengan syaitan. Nik Aziz dan pemimpin PAS yang lain sanggup mengeluarkan kata-kata yang buruk kononnya Badawi Malaysia menjadi gembala babi. Sindiran ini tidak mempunyai asas kerana Abdullah Badawi telah ditugaskan untuk menyelaraskan kerja-kerja menghapuskan penyakit JE (Japanese Encephalitis), bukan untuk menjaga babi. Lebih dari itu dakwaan dibuat kononnya tuhan mencarut dan kita orang Islam patut mencarut.

"Tetapi orang PAS akan terus setia kepada PAS kerana mereka fanatik dan taasub kepada parti mereka. Mereka adalah daripada kumpulan asabiyah, kumpulan yang terlalu fanatik dalam menyokong kumpulan mereka sehingga tidak mengambilkira kumpulan mereka baik atau jahat, benar atau salah. Demikian apabila ahli PAS berkhalwat, mereka tidak bersalah. Kesalahan hanya ada pada orang lain, tidak sama sekali kepada orang PAS dan parti PAS. Inilah orang yang keterlaluan dan termasuk dalam golongan asabiyah."

Mahathir cukup benar bacaannya tentang PAS serta ahli-ahli yang mempunyai sentimen kefanatikan yang cukup besar. Sikap ini bukan sahaja ada pada golongan tidak berpendidikan tinggi, golongan kelas pertengahan dan akademik berjawatan tinggi di universiti pun sama saja kefanatikan mereka.

Saya menyokong PAS selama 20 tahun, sebagai ahli dan penyumbang wang serta pemikiran. Saya juga membenci semua tuduhan Mahathir terhadap PAS dahulu, tetapi hari ini saya terpaksa mengakui bahawa bacaan Mahathir tentang PAS ternyata benar dan saya dapat melihat dengan sendiri kebenaran tersebut hari ini.

Sebagai ringkasan ucapan Mahathir di atas, beliau membawa mesej tentang bahaya kepercayaan fanatik kepada agama dan parti politik yang boleh merosakkan orang Melayu dan pembinaan negara bangsa serta pembangunan ekonomi untuk semua.

b879995cf1e26209: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks.

The missions affected by the outages—hopefully temporary—are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001 and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history.

The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate.
44f6d57a797b432e: According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters, Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide.

Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote.

The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's post-incident report, dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident.
1479a2d5f1158c80: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset.

It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math.

The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. This gives it significance for areas ranging from number theory to cryptography. As Wikipedia accurately states, "It is considered by pure mathematicians to be one of the most important problems in the field."

73155e0b93283f09: Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water.

The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23. Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died.

On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death, an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child. New York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby. On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a child between the age of 0 and 4.
58c64dd3bfb5f2ac: In 2017, Apple removed the home button from its iPhones. Users lost a convenient, tangible control — part of a larger shift to digital buttons, knobs, and sliders we also see in cars (like with radio presets and air conditioning) and kitchens (see smart fridges). We can’t leave physical controls behind entirely, though. They tend to be more convenient and efficient — think of how you can use a physical gaming controller without looking at it — and, at times, more precise, like when you use a dial to get the volume just right. But tangible controls are typically preprogrammed to do a specific thing, minimizing their usefulness. A new system called “TangiMap,” co-developed by an MIT graduate student and researcher at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), helps bring tangible control back to your software. The system personalizes the physical controls on everyday devices by mapping digital widgets onto tangible inputs, turning things like editing photos, animation, performing music, and creating 3D models into more dynamic and tactile experiences. Just as a DJ’s pads switch between triggering cues, loops, and samples, TangiMap gives a device’s controls entirely new roles. But how, exactly? TangiMap relies on an AI agent, or semi-autonomous programs that “think” and complete well-defined tasks, to find and act on context about the software you’re using, your tendencies, and the device used to control that program. To gather the required context, the agent can draw on sources such as the program’s API (the rules that let programs talk to each other), an MCP server (a standard that connects AI agents to apps), or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model. Then, the agent uses a large language model to put all the info it's gathered into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls. “TangiMap builds on our broader vision of reprogramming common objects to be more dynamic,” says Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21, a doctoral student in the MIT Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science and a CSAIL researcher whose advisor is MIT Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller. “Here, AI agents help us adapt physical controls to whatever we’re working on. We want to bring back physical controls so we can interact with our devices eyes-free, the way you adjust a car’s volume without looking away from the road. Physical controls also let you adjust several settings at once, like tweaking brightness and contrast together when editing an image, which is hard to do on a screen.” The system helped the researchers turn a standard mixer into a photo-editing controller. That way, they could adjust color in Adobe Lightroom, with a complementary visualization of those controls displayed on their screen. The team did the same with sound-mixing software, so that performers can adjust their music in real-time with their own inputs to knobs and faders.  The researchers also reprogrammed a simpler mixer to work with the 3D modeling program Blender. Their interface included an area where users can type in a prompt, and once the model was generated, users could adjust features like shininess on a mixer using physical controls. Within Adobe’s Character Animator software, TangiMap connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad so users could animate (or “puppeteer”) a cartoon character live. Zhu and co-author Chang Xiao, an assistant professor at Boston University, presented their tool at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology earlier this month. Zhu and Xiao created a custom user interface (UI) for each application. While that adds another layer of personalization to the creative process, the team is hoping to create a more streamlined system that helps the designer to generate the UI for their device by taking a picture. The researchers are also considering the physical aspects of user interactions. They want to use more ergonomic devices and also ensure that TangiMap accounts for where users position their hands when doing different tasks. For example, users typically hold a mixer differently when they’re using it to make music than, say, when playing a video game. You may want controls mapped closer or further apart, depending on what you’re doing. Zhu is hoping to do a user study to get more feedback about TangiMap, and whether this kind of “smart DJing” could indeed improve those experiences. But the dynamic reprogramming she ultimately envisions is even more ambitious. “The same way our phones and computers generalize to a range of tasks, we want other objects to be more intelligent,” she says. “I would like to build physical items that use an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into. They could understand what to transform into, given a specific situation.” A chemical jar, for instance, could tell you if it’s sealed correctly when asked, and when you want to see what it’s typically used for, the container would instead display that information. While that kind of versatility and interactivity is a ways off, more powerful agents and more intricate fabrication pipelines could bring everyday objects to life. Their work was supported, in part, by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.
e41a71b86838ecc4: Extraordinarily harsh droughts and heavy flooding have become more common around the globe this year due to an unusually strong El Niño. AP Photo/Charlie RiedelThe extreme weather fueled by an unusually intense El Niño has caused flooding in low-lying Florida communities, hammered the California coast and upended hurricane patterns – just to name a few examples. But it also poses a growing challenge for companies that need timely climate data to manage supply chains. This information is disappearing due to federal budget cuts, leaving businesses less prepared to handle the impact of extreme weather. To be sure, forecasters saw the 2026 El Niño coming. The Climate Prediction Center at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, has been forecasting a very strong El Niño since the spring, and its October update put the odds at 83% that this El Niño will become the strongest since record-keeping began in 1950, likely lasting into early 2027. That kind of warning is valuable. It gives companies months to stock up, reroute shipments and line up backup suppliers before storms arrive or droughts set in. But bit by bit, other valuable sources of climate data are getting cut. That includes a federal database on disasters, which adds up costs weeks after the event, that NOAA stopped updating in May 2025. The Trump administration has also cut or undercut federal climate analyses, as well as staff and funding for daily forecasting, which has left large parts of the country without coverage during extreme events – a risky prospect for businesses. As a scholar of business operations and sustainability, I believe these cuts could have cascading effects on companies and supply chains by leaving them more vulnerable to future weather disasters. Eventually, these disruptions will hit consumers as well through higher prices. Gaps in climate science grow In North America, El Niño weather patterns are linked to severe storms in the Pacific, as well as floods, fires and droughts. The economic hit can be substantial, from transportation delays to massive crop failures. Strong El Niño events have historically cost the global economy trillions of dollars. This El Niño arrives as the pace of natural disasters picks up. While the U.S. averaged fewer than five “billion-dollar” disasters a year in the 1980s, that number now stands above 20 a year – a huge leap, even accounting for inflation. And the 2023 and 2024 totals were the highest on record. While the scope of weather damage gets worse and worse, critical data is missing. That includes NOAA’s decision to retire its “Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters” database, ending updates after 2024. For more than four decades, it tracked the cost of U.S. weather disasters after the fact – and businesses and researchers alike have relied on it to build prediction models. For example, scientists use these historical records to put odds on future losses or to forecast economic activity. Some of my own research also relies on historically accurate climate and weather data. Unfortunately, the gap in climate science may be widening. In 2025 the federal government shut down Climate.gov, which served as a central repository for weather and climate data, while its El Niño blog has been frozen since June 2025. The National Climate Assessments, the U.S. government’s preeminent reports on climate science, were taken offline, while the National Weather Service cited staff shortages as it cut back weather balloon launches at multiple sites, which feed forecast models. Fortunately, some of these data-gathering efforts have migrated elsewhere. The scientists behind the El Niño blog have moved to a nonprofit, while another nonprofit is carrying on the efforts behind the billion-dollar disaster database. El Nino’s effects, especially strong in 2026, have disrupted crops and supply chains around the world, including a delayed monsoon season in India. Ashish Vaishnav/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images What this means for supply chains The Trump administration has justified these cuts by citing high administrative costs and potential errors in the prediction models. But that still leaves companies, which lean on public weather data more than most shoppers realize, scrambling. In many industries, including retail, food processing and agriculture, the payoff from acting early to safeguard supply chains can be large. Real-time and near-real-time data is used in supply chains for enhancing crop yields, finding the best routes for transport, inventory planning, and ensuring worker safety during weather emergencies. For example, Walmart invests heavily in technology and specialists to monitor weather-related disruptions and build resilient supply chains. Another example is insurance companies, which use weather data for designing commercial insurance policies and processing claims. Risk Management Solutions Inc., a leading catastrophe risk-modeling company owned by Moody’s Corp., regularly use NOAA’s hurricane datasets to inform its advanced risk models. When public climate data disappears, companies still need timely information to run their supply chains, so some will pay for alternative data. This typically comes from paid private services and subscriptions. Startups such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone offer private weather balloon data and advanced climate prediction services. While privatization can fill some gaps, it’s usually only the large retailers and insurers who can afford these forecasts. Smaller suppliers, local farmers and independent truckers further up the supply chain often can’t. And that’s exactly where many disruptions begin. What it means for consumers Shoppers feel these disruptions when shortages feed into higher prices, often months later. In 2024, for example, extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, pushed U.S. orange juice prices to an all-time high that fall. They have have stayed elevated since hurricanes Helene and Milton battered Florida’s groves. Holiday staples are also not spared. A 2021 heat dome in the Pacific Northwest led to major damage to Christmas tree farms, causing their prices to rise an additional 5% to 10% that year. And these effects are often global. Poor rains in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, and that inflation is still feeding into U.S. chocolate prices, which were up 14% in 2026. A historic El Niño, arriving just as federal climate data becomes sparse, makes this winter an ideal, if unfortunate, test of what climate information is really worth.
